desktop.d01: Every year, India sends lakhs of crores of rupees directly into citizens' bank accounts. Yet millions of eligible families never receive what is rightfully theirs. This is Sahayak, and this is how we designed it.
desktop.d02: We listened to the people these schemes are meant for. Four barriers kept coming up. Portals speak English and official Hindi, not the language people think in. Forms are full of jargon. Middlemen charge hundreds of rupees for help that should be free. And after applying, the application disappears into a black box.
desktop.d03: So we designed for real people. Rameshwar, a farmer who cannot type. Lakshmi, a domestic worker who loses a day's wages for every wrong queue. Arindam, a weaver who needs a small loan. And Sunita, a student who applies for six relatives from one phone.
desktop.d04: That gave us five principles. Speak first, read second. Show the money. One decision per screen. Always say what comes next. And make trust a feature, not a footnote.
desktop.d05: Our colours come straight from the Sahayak emblem. Navy, from the shield, means trust, and carries text and navigation. Orange, from the people, means warmth and action, so it is reserved for the single most important action on each screen. Teal, from the speech bubble, means help and success. It all sits on a calm neutral canvas, and every text colour passes accessibility contrast, by day and by night.
desktop.d06: Type had to work in thirteen languages and ten scripts. We pair Plus Jakarta Sans, which matches our wordmark, with Google's Noto Sans for every Indian script, and Noto Nastaliq for Urdu. Only the font for your language is downloaded, so the app stays fast on low cost phones.
desktop.d07: Let's see it live. The first screen greets you in every Indian language, over a photograph of the people we serve.
desktop.d08: Next, you choose your language. Each one is written in its own script, with a speaker button, so someone who cannot read can hear it before choosing.
desktop.d09: Three short screens explain what Sahayak does, ending with our most important promise. Applying is free, and nobody should charge you.
desktop.d10: This is home. At the top is the most natural way to ask for help: tap and speak. Just below, four facts build trust at a glance.
desktop.d11: Every welfare journey has five steps: find, check, papers, apply and track. Most portals hide this. We draw it as a thread, so a family always knows what is done, and what comes next.
desktop.d12: Schemes are organised by what is happening in your life, not by ministry names. Real photographs make each need recognisable, even without reading.
desktop.d13: Signing in is optional. Sahayak works fully as a guest, and nothing leaves the phone. The sign in sheet says this plainly, before asking for anything.
desktop.d14: Voice is the heart of Sahayak. The assistant listens in your language, and answers with clear next steps. Here, a farmer describes his situation, and is guided straight to the right check.
desktop.d15: The eligibility check asks one plain question per screen, with large answers you can tap, or say aloud. It moves forward on its own, and you can always go back.
desktop.d16: Results lead with the money. Yearly cash is shown separately from hospital cover and loans, so nothing is exaggerated. Schemes that need one more document are explained, never hidden.
desktop.d17: Each scheme page opens with what you get, who can apply, the papers you need, and how long the office may take. The government fee, zero rupees, sits right next to the most a help centre may charge.
desktop.d18: Rejected documents are the biggest cause of delay. So Sahayak checks your papers before you leave home. The camera looks for blur, glare and missing corners, and explains how to fix a bad photo.
desktop.d19: When you are ready, choose how to apply. Sahayak makes a printable slip with a QR code, a checklist, and the fee promise in writing.
desktop.d20: After applying, the tracker shows which step you are on, and how many days the office has left by law. If something is late, or someone asks for money, you can raise a complaint in one tap, in your own language.
desktop.d21: Sahayak also finds help centres nearby, shows whether they are open right now, and which languages are spoken there.
desktop.d22: Accessibility is built in. Text can be made larger. Night mode is gentle on the eyes. Sunlight mode gives maximum contrast outdoors. And data saver removes images and effects for older phones.
desktop.d23: For operators who help dozens of people a day, a command palette opens any scheme or action from the keyboard.
desktop.d24: And every word adapts to your language. Hindi. Kannada. Even Urdu, which turns the whole interface from right to left.
desktop.d25: Sahayak. Thirteen languages. Voice first. Free forever. Built so that no family ever has to pay a middleman for what is already theirs. Thank you.

mobile.m01: Sahayak on mobile. Most of the people we design for will only ever use a low cost Android phone, so this is where the design had to be at its very best.
mobile.m02: The first run is calm and swipeable. A greeting in your language, a language picker you can listen to, and three illustrated promises.
mobile.m03: Navigation lives in the thumb zone. Four destinations sit in the dock, and the speak button is raised in the centre, because voice is the primary input.
mobile.m04: Home leads with a real photograph and a single invitation: tap and speak. As you scroll, the top bar slides away to give content the whole screen, and returns the moment you scroll back.
mobile.m05: The assistant opens as a bottom sheet, right in the thumb zone. It listens, shows your words, and answers with a button to the next step.
mobile.m06: The eligibility check is one question per screen, with answer cards large enough for calloused or trembling fingers.
mobile.m07: Results count up to what your family could receive, and the summary can be shared straight to WhatsApp, where information really travels in a village.
mobile.m08: On a scheme page, the main action waits in a sticky bar just above the dock, always within reach of the thumb.
mobile.m09: Papers are checked before you leave home, which saves a second trip, and a day's wages.
mobile.m10: The help centre slip puts the fee promise in writing. Zero rupees to the government. At most thirty rupees for help.
mobile.m11: Tracking shows the four official stages and the legal time limit, with anything urgent shown first.
mobile.m12: One phone often serves a whole family. Sahayak checks for each family member separately, so answers never get mixed up.
mobile.m13: Outdoors, sunlight mode switches to maximum contrast in one tap. Text size scales every screen, and data saver keeps things fast on slow networks.
mobile.m14: And when you change language, everything changes instantly. Every button, every scheme, every sentence.
mobile.m15: Sahayak. Help, offered, in the language you think in.
